hints: Focus on what type of hydrolysis this is, alkaline with excess NaOH, not acidic with water or dilute acid.
Split the diester at the two C-O single bonds of the ester links to see the three fragments, a C1 acid part, a C3 diol part, and a C2 acid part.
Remember acids are neutralised to sodium salts by NaOH, but alcohols stay as alcohols in aqueous NaOH, then match that pattern.
walkthrough:
**Spot the two ester groups**

Look carefully at the starting molecule. It has two ester links, $R-C(=O)-O-R'$. On the left you have $H-C(=O)-O-CH_2-$, a methanoate ester. On the right you have $CH_3-C(=O)-O-CH_2-$, an ethanoate ester. In the middle you have $-CH_2-CH_2-CH_2-$, which will become a diol.

General alkaline hydrolysis:
$$RCOOR' + NaOH \rightarrow RCOONa + R'OH$$

**Recall alkaline vs acid hydrolysis**

This is a really important distinction. Acid hydrolysis gives carboxylic acid + alcohol. Alkaline hydrolysis with NaOH gives carboxylate salt + alcohol. Since we are heating with excess aqueous $NaOH$, any $-COOH$ formed is immediately neutralised to $-COONa$.

**Apply to both ends of the diester**

Break the left ester: $HCOO-CH_2- + NaOH \rightarrow HCOONa$ (sodium methanoate) + $HO-CH_2-$. Break the right ester: $-CH_2-OOCCH_3 + NaOH \rightarrow CH_3COONa$ (sodium ethanoate) + $-CH_2-OH$. Put the middle together and you get $HO-CH_2-CH_2-CH_2-OH$, propane-1,3-diol.

**Check the alcohol does not change**

A common worry is whether the $OH$ groups of the diol also react with NaOH to give $ONa$. They do not under these aqueous conditions. Alcohols are very weak acids and stay as $R-OH$. So the final set is two sodium carboxylates plus one free diol.

options.A: Shows methanoic acid, propane-1,3-diol and ethanoic acid. This is the result of acid hydrolysis with water or dilute acid, not alkaline hydrolysis. With excess NaOH the acids would be neutralised to their sodium salts.
options.B: Shows free carboxylic acids but the diol as a disodium alkoxide, $NaO-CH_2-CH_2-CH_2-ONa$. This is backwards. Acids do react with NaOH, alcohols do not in aqueous solution. So the acids should be salts and the diol should stay as HO-CH2-CH2-CH2-OH.
options.C: Shows sodium methanoate $HCOONa$, propane-1,3-diol $HOCH_2CH_2CH_2OH$, and sodium ethanoate $CH_3COONa$. This is exactly correct for alkaline hydrolysis of this unsymmetrical diester, both ester links cleaved, acids neutralised, alcohol released unchanged.
options.D: Shows both carboxylate salts correctly but also shows the diol as $NaO-CH_2-CH_2-CH_2-ONa$. This is the trap of thinking every OH reacts with NaOH. Alcohols are too weakly acidic to form stable alkoxides in water, only the carboxylic acids form sodium salts here.
